title: Beating the Sicilian: the Alapin
standfirst: Half your opponents will meet 1.e4 with 1…c5. You can spend years learning the Open Sicilian, or you can play 2.c3 and get a good game with one idea.

steps.title: The problem with the Sicilian
body: 1…c5 fights for the centre without blocking anything, and the main lines run twenty-five moves deep in places. That's a lot to learn for a move your opponent plays automatically.
The Alapin's whole idea fits in one sentence: build the big centre anyway.

steps.title: An asymmetrical fight
body: Black stakes a claim on d4 from the side rather than mirroring. He doesn't get equal central space, but he gets the half-open c-file and unbalanced play — which is exactly what a Sicilian player is after.

steps.title: Preparing d4 the slow way
body: The Alapin. White intends d2–d4, and c3 will be there to recapture, giving him the broad pawn centre the Sicilian is designed to prevent.
The cost is real: c3 takes the natural square from the b1 knight. That's the trade — a slightly awkward knight for a big centre and almost no theory.

steps.title: Black strikes first
body: The critical reply, and the one you'll face most. Instead of allowing d4, Black hits e4 immediately while White's queenside knight has nowhere good to go.

steps.title: Take
body: Nothing better — and this is the point of the next move.

steps.title: The queen comes out too early
body: Black must recapture with the queen; …Nf6 costs a pawn for insufficient play. But an early queen is a target, and White's next move exploits exactly that.

steps.title: The big centre arrives
body: There it is. White has the centre he wanted, c3 supports it, and — crucially — every piece White develops from here comes out hitting the black queen.

steps.title: Get the pieces out
body: Black sensibly develops rather than grabbing anything. The queen will have to move again soon.

steps.title: Natural and useful
body: Developing toward the centre and guarding d4. Notice how easy White's moves are to find — that's the appeal of this system.

steps.title: Open the bishop
body: Black prepares to develop the dark-squared bishop and castle. Solid and unhurried.

steps.title: Modest, then castle
body: The bishop takes a quiet square rather than an ambitious one. There is no rush: White's structure is better and the game is long.

steps.title: A comfortable game with no memorisation
body: White castles next and has a pleasant position: more central space and easy development, against a Sicilian player who never got the Sicilian.
The plan from here is simple — finish developing, and consider d4–d5 at the right moment to open the position while you're better placed for it.
